sections.h2: Does Texas tax profit from selling a house?
sections.html:
Texas does not tax it. The Comptroller's office states that Texas has no state income tax, so a home sale adds nothing to a state return because there is no state return to file.

The federal government is the only income tax collector in a Texas home sale. Texas homeowners still deal with property taxes at closing, covered below, but those are charges for owning the house and not a tax on profit.

sections.h2: How much gain can a Texas seller exclude from federal tax?
sections.html:
Up to $250,000 of gain from the sale of a main home, or up to $500,000 on a joint return with a spouse, according to IRS Topic 701. The exclusion applies to the gain, which is the sale price less your adjusted basis and selling costs, and it does not apply to the whole price.

Basis is generally what you paid, plus sales tax and purchase expenses. IRS Topic 703 adds that improvements raise basis and items such as insurance reimbursements for casualty losses lower it. Keep receipts for roofs, additions and similar work, because they reduce the gain you report.

Texas sellers should also know that losses on a personal residence are not deductible. Topic 409 says losses from the sale of personal-use property such as a home or car do not lower your taxes.

sections.h2: What tests must a Texas seller pass to claim the exclusion?
sections.html:
You must pass an ownership test and a use test, both measured over the five years ending on the sale date. The IRS describes the details this way.

Federal home-sale exclusion tests, IRS Topic 701
ItemWhat the IRS says
OwnershipOwned the home at least 24 months out of the last 5 years
UseLived in it as a residence at least 24 months of the previous 5 years
TimingThe two periods may fall in different stretches of the 5 years
Joint filersEither spouse meets ownership; both spouses meet use
Repeat useGenerally not allowed if you excluded gain on another home in the prior two years
Military and similar serviceMay elect to suspend the five-year period for up to 10 years

Source: irs.gov/taxtopics/tc701. Publication 523 has the complete eligibility rules and the exceptions to the two-year requirement.

sections.h2: What rates apply to gain above the exclusion?
sections.html:
Gain above the exclusion is a long-term capital gain if you held the house more than one year, and the federal rate depends on your taxable income. The IRS prints the 2025 tax-year brackets on Topic 409.

  • 0 percent when taxable income is at or below $48,350 for single filers and married filing separately, $96,700 for married filing jointly, or $64,750 for head of household.
  • 15 percent above those amounts, up to $533,400 for single, $300,000 for married filing separately, $600,050 for married filing jointly, or $566,700 for head of household.
  • 20 percent on the amount of taxable income above the 15 percent ceilings.

Topic 409 also says some unrecaptured section 1250 gain is taxed at up to 25 percent, which can matter if part of the house was rented out and depreciated. Net short-term gains, from property held one year or less, are taxed as ordinary income. These figures are for the 2025 tax year, so check the IRS page for the year in which your Texas sale closes.

sections.h2: What about an inherited house or a house that was a rental?
sections.html:
Both cases change the math, and neither fits the simple exclusion story. For inherited property, the IRS says basis comes from Publication 551 instead of the cost to the owner. Topic 409 notes that special holding-period rules exist for property acquired from a decedent and sends readers to Publication 544.

For a former rental, depreciation lowers basis, and the unrecaptured section 1250 rule may apply to that portion. Publication 523 covers home sales with business or rental use.

If you inherited the house and want to understand the title side first, see the Texas affidavit of heirship and probate pages on this site.

sections.h2: Do I have to report the sale if all the gain is excluded?
sections.html:
Sometimes yes. The IRS says that if you receive Form 1099-S, you must report the sale even when the gain is fully excludable. You must also report it if you cannot exclude all of your gain.

When reporting applies, use Form 8949 and Schedule D of Form 1040. A seller who financed the sale over several years may use the installment method, and Topic 701 says the home-sale exclusion remains available alongside it.

Estimated tax payments can be required when a taxable gain is large. The IRS points to Publication 505 for that rule.

sections.h2: Which Texas costs still come up at closing?
sections.html:
Property tax is the main one. The Comptroller says no Texas tax is levied by the state on property, and that local units set rates and collect it. Appraisal districts value property as of January 1, and bills usually go out in October.

The tax lien attaches on January 1 for that year's taxes, so a buyer cannot get clear title until delinquent taxes are paid. Delinquency starts February 1 for most bills, with a six percent penalty and one percent interest. Ask the title company for the tax certificate and the proration figure for the closing date, and the county tax assessor-collector for the exact balance.

faqs.q: Is there a Texas capital gains tax on real estate?
faqs.a: No. The Comptroller states that Texas has no state income tax, so a home sale produces no state capital gains return. The federal rules in IRS Topic 701 and Topic 409 still apply.

faqs.q: How long must I live in a Texas home to avoid federal tax on the gain?
faqs.a: At least 24 months of the 5 years before the sale, and you must have owned it for 24 months of that period too. The months do not have to be consecutive, and the ownership and use periods can differ.

faqs.q: What is the exclusion for a married couple selling a Texas house?
faqs.a: Up to $500,000 of gain on a joint return. Either spouse may meet the ownership test, but both must meet the use test individually, per IRS Topic 701.

faqs.q: Can I deduct a loss when I sell my Texas home for less than I paid?
faqs.a: No. IRS Topic 409 says losses from the sale of personal-use property, including your home, are not tax deductible.

faqs.q: Where do I report a Texas home sale?
faqs.a: On Form 8949 and Schedule D of Form 1040 when reporting is required, which includes cases where you receive Form 1099-S. Publication 523 has the worksheets. A tax professional can confirm what applies to your situation.
